opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Habakkuk 1:12–2:4 — When We Do Not Understand What God Is Doing

The reading from the Book of Habakkuk begins with a man who believes deeply in God but cannot understand what God is allowing to happen.

Habakkuk is looking at the violence, corruption, and injustice within Judah. He has already asked God why He permits it. God tells him that the Babylonians, a powerful and ruthless nation, will be used to bring judgment upon Judah. This answer troubles Habakkuk even more. How could a holy and merciful God allow a nation even more violent than Judah to become the instrument of judgment?

Habakkuk does not pretend to understand. He questions God directly, but he does something important first: he reminds himself of who God is. God is eternal. God is holy. God is his Rock. Habakkuk cannot reconcile what he sees happening with what he knows to be true about God.

Then Habakkuk waits.

He says that he will take his place at the watchtower and watch for God’s answer. He does not turn away because he is confused or angry. He brings his questions to God and remains there long enough to listen.

God answers him by telling him to write down the vision because it concerns an appointed time. It may seem slow in coming, but God tells him, “If it delays, wait for it.” And then comes the statement that carries through the rest of Scripture: “The just one shall live by faith.”

God does not give Habakkuk an explanation for every suffering he is witnessing. Instead, He assures him that evil will not continue without consequence and that what appears to be God’s silence is not God’s absence.

There is mercy even in God’s judgment. God had not stopped loving His people because they had turned away from Him. He was calling them back. He would not simply abandon them to the corruption that was destroying them. Even Babylon, which appeared for a time to be unstoppable, would eventually answer for its own violence and pride.

This is an important distinction. God’s mercy does not mean that He ignores what destroys us. Sometimes His mercy is found in His refusal to leave us unchanged by it. He corrects, disciplines, waits, calls us back, and continues working toward something we may not yet be able to see.

Habakkuk teaches us that faith does not require pretending that everything makes sense. We can ask God difficult questions. We can tell Him when we do not understand. But then we have to remain with Him long enough to hear His answer.

There will be times when we are standing where Habakkuk stood—seeing only what is happening today while God already knows where the story is going.

That is when His instruction becomes ours:

Wait for it. Remain faithful. God has not abandoned His people, and what we see today is not necessarily the end of the story.
